El primer ensayo clínico controlado docu: The first documented controlled clinical trial was run by James Lind in 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury. He took twelve sailors with scurvy in a similar state, split them into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy: cider, vitriol, vinegar, sea water, a paste of herbs, and two oranges with a lemon. The citrus cured them. What is remarkable is not the result —it was already suspected— but the design: same ship, same food, same initial state, six treatments in parallel. What was missing, and would take two centuries to arrive, was the draw: randomisation was introduced by Ronald Fisher in the 1920s, and not in medicine but in agriculture, assigning fertilisers at random among plots of a field.
El razonamiento es este. Si el paciente,: The reasoning is this. If the patient, the doctor or biased chance decides who goes into each group, the groups will differ in the treatment and in other things. If a coin decides it, the groups differ in the treatment and in nothing else, but noise: age, diet, income, genetics and the hundred factors you have not even thought of are shared out equally between the two, because the coin knows nothing about them.

If you measure twenty variables and publish the one that came out significant, you have manufactured a finding out of nothing: with twenty tests at 5 %, one comes out “significant” by pure chance. Declaring in advance what will be measured is what prevents that game, and its absence explains a good part of the scientific results that could not later be reproduced.
